summary.one_liner: Lessons from running HubSpot's 5 Whys post-mortems: frame failures as systems problems, favor recovery (MTTR) over prevention, avoid "be less stupid" and "slow down" fixes, and facilitate for consensus.
keywords: how to run a 5 whys session
takeaways: Frame post-mortem fixes around the broadest class of future problems instead of hunting a single root cause.
Prioritize fast detection and recovery (MTTR) over trying to prevent every failure (MTBF).
Avoid answers like 'be less careful' or 'slow down'; assume future people will be as fallible as today's and fix the system.
As facilitator, frame the incident in customer and economic terms, use a whiteboard, draw in quiet attendees, and keep the group in one room (about eight people max).
summary.summary: This HubSpot engineering blog post reflects on fifty-plus 5 Whys post-mortems modeled on Eric Ries's method. The author argues that failures come from systems rather than individual developers, that there is rarely a single root cause, and that recovery speed matters more than prevention. It shares examples such as the product quality crisis, where the post-mortems showed that monitoring and deploy processes were the problem, and notes how the team handled an EC2 outage. It closes with practical facilitation tips: frame the bad event in customer impact terms, build consensus on a whiteboard, and hold the meeting in person.
